readerTitle: Two founders, one kitchen: how to split the business without breaking it
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (사무실 점심 케이터링: 식음료 + B2B 서비스) · 인물과 수치는 모두 설명용
insight: 지분 나누기는 '몇 대 몇'이라는 결정 하나가 아니다. 얼마나 갖는지, 어떻게 얻는지, 누가 무엇을 정하는지, 누가 통제하는지를 따로 정해야 하는 네 가지 결정이다.
misconception: 공동창업자끼리 비율만 공정하게 정하면 끝이고, 지분이 많은 사람이 모든 결정을 하는 게 당연하다.

sources.text: 창업 실무의 일반 개념 (공동창업자 지분 배분, 베스팅과 클리프, 의사결정 권한, 소유와 통제의 구분)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: '4년 베스팅 + 1년 클리프가 스타트업에서 흔히 쓰인다'는 표현은 업계 관행에 대한 일반적 서술입니다. 특정 비율이나 통계를 주장하지 않도록 문구를 유지했는지 확인하세요.
지분 55/45, 투자 제안 $50,000에 20% 등은 모두 가상 수치입니다. 지분 계약, 베스팅, 투자자 권리는 나라마다 법과 세무 처리가 다르므로 7번 카드에서 현지 전문가 상담을 권하는 문장을 유지하세요 (법률 조언 아님).

cards.title: Two founders, one kitchen, zero paperwork.
body: Lena is a chef who has run weekend catering from a rented kitchen for eight months. Omar sells services to companies and knows dozens of office managers.
Together they want to deliver lunches to offices. They shake hands on Friday. On Monday they need to decide who owns what. You'll make four calls for them.

image.label: Two founders at a kitchen counter with lunch boxes and a blank contract
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 업소용 주방 조리대 위에 도시락 상자들이 쌓여 있고, 셰프 복장의 여성과 셔츠 차림의 남성이 서로 마주 보고 있음. 둘 사이에 아무것도 적히지 않은 계약서 한 장과 펜. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How should they split ownership?
body: Lena brings recipes, a few clients and is full-time today. Omar brings sales contacts but can only join full-time in six months. Neither is putting in much cash.

options.text: 50/50. They're partners, so keep it equal and simple
options.feedback: It avoids an awkward talk today. But it ignores the six-month gap, and two equal owners can deadlock with no way out.

options.text: 70/30 for Lena. She started it and the recipes are hers
options.feedback: It rewards eight weekend months over the years of work ahead. Omar may start to feel like an employee, and his sales effort is what grows the business.

options.text: Talk through what each will bring over the next four years, then agree a split
options.feedback: Harder conversation, better outcome. They weigh time, skills, risk and the late start, and land on 55/45 that both can explain out loud.

cards.title: Say you chose to talk it through. Now: what if someone leaves?
body: They agree on 55/45. A month later, Omar's start date slips. Lena wonders: if he walks away next year, does he keep 45% of a business she built?

options.text: Write nothing down. They trust each other
options.feedback: Trust is real, but plans change. If either leaves, the other could carry a silent owner for years, and fixing it later costs money and friendship.

options.text: Both earn their shares month by month over four years, with nothing earned before the first year
options.feedback: This is vesting with a one-year cliff. Whoever leaves early keeps only what they earned, and the rule protects both, not just Lena.

options.text: Only Omar's shares are earned over time. Lena owns hers now
options.feedback: It protects Lena from Omar leaving, but not Omar from Lena leaving. One-sided terms often breed resentment. Crediting her past work with a small upfront portion is fairer.

cards.title: Say you chose shared vesting. Then comes the first fight.
body: A large law firm will sign a year-long contract if the menu gets cheaper. Omar wants to say yes. Lena says cheaper ingredients will hurt quality. Who decides?

options.text: Lena. She owns 55%, so she has the final word
options.feedback: Owning more doesn't have to mean deciding everything. If Omar loses every disagreement, he soon stops selling hard.

options.text: Split areas: Lena owns menu and kitchen, Omar owns pricing and contracts. Big deals need both, with an agreed tie-breaker
options.feedback: Each founder moves fast in their lane. Here, Omar negotiates price while Lena designs a cheaper menu she can stand behind.
Fair in theory. With two people, a vote is either a stalemate or the bigger owner always winning.

cards.title: Say you chose clear lanes. Now a friend offers money.
body: To buy a delivery van, a family friend offers $50,000 for 20% of the business. One condition: she must approve any spending over $500.

options.feedback: Twenty percent of the profits is fine. A veto on almost every purchase hands her control of daily operations.

options.text: Take the money, but limit her say to big decisions like selling the business or raising more money
options.feedback: They get the van and keep running the business. She still gets protection where it matters most to her money.
Full control is kept, but growth slows while they save for the van. Sometimes that's the right trade. It's a choice, not a rule.

cards.title: Four decisions, not one number.
body: Most founders think splitting a business means agreeing a ratio. Lena and Omar actually made four separate decisions: **how much** each owns, **how they earn it**, who decides what, and who controls the company.
Each answer solved a different problem. A perfect ratio would not have stopped the first fight, and lanes would not have helped if Omar had walked away.

image.label: Four labeled building blocks: share, vesting, decision rights, control
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일 블록 네 개가 계단처럼 쌓여 있음. 각 블록에 "How much", "How it's earned", "Who decides", "Who controls" 라벨. 맨 위에 작은 도시락 배달 밴. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Paper helps, but it isn't the partnership.
body: No split is perfectly fair, and roles shift as a business grows. Plan to revisit lanes once a year, not just when something breaks.
Rules for ownership and vesting also differ by country. Use this lesson to prepare the conversation, then have a local lawyer write it up.
cards.softwareNote: The same four decisions apply in software startups. Four-year vesting with a one-year cliff is common there, and investors often check founder vesting before they invest.

cards.title: Split the business in four layers, before you need to.
body: Each call you made maps to one idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1 → Splitting ownership:** base it on future contribution, not just the past
**Decision 2 → Vesting:** earn shares over time, with rules that protect everyone
**Decision 3 → Roles and decision rights:** give each founder a lane and a tie-breaker
**Decision 4 → Ownership vs control:** a small stake can carry big control, so negotiate both
cards.callout: **Try it today:** if you have a partner, write one sentence for each layer. Where you can't, that's your next conversation.
